effects.verbatim: Multiple logistic regression (forward stepwise method) with having at least one child (N = 257 men) or no children (N = 242 men) as a dependent variable, educational level as a categorical predictor, and current age, number of siblings, birth order, height, and facial attractiveness defined as continuous predictors showed that the probability of parenthood was significantly higher in facially more attractive and better educated men (Wald's χ² = 12.97 and 8.76, df = 1 and 2, P = 0.0003 and 0.012, respectively).

Education is the only status-type proxy in this paper (no income/wealth/occupation measured); the paper's primary predictor of interest is facial attractiveness (a mate-value/genetic-quality cue), not status, so this is a secondary covariate result. Reported statistic is a Wald chi-square for a categorical (df=2) predictor in a logistic regression on a binary 'any children' outcome — no per-level OR/beta or SE is given for this specific model (contrast with Table 2, which does give per-level logistic estimates but for a different outcome, probability of marriage, not fertility). Cannot be converted to r without more info; flagging needs_pi. When restricted to married men only (or married men with ≥1 child), the paper states the backward-stepwise regression 'was not significant' overall, with no coefficients reported at all. reason_if_not: Pure theoretical/simulation paper (Rogers, "More Status or More Children? Social Status, Fertility Reduction, and Long-Term Fitness," Evolution and Human Behavior 1999). Presents a formal fitness-tradeoff model showing reduced fertility can be an evolved strategy to maximize long-term fitness under recurrent demographic-crash risk (diverting resources from offspring production to survivorship). No empirical sample, no status measure, and no status->reproduction correlation/regression is reported. Retrieved file is a paywalled ScienceDirect landing page with abstract only (no full text/tables), but the abstract itself is sufficient to confirm the theoretical/simulation design and absence of any extractable status-fertility effect.

Only the ScienceDirect abstract/landing page was retrievable for this file (the __PRELOADED_STATE__ JSON contains only an 'abstracts' key plus paywall/entitlement markers; no full-text sections, methods, or tables are present). Independent of retrieval, the paper's actual predictor is facial attractiveness (a morphological/physical trait) predicting age-specific reproduction/lifetime reproductive success in rural Senegal and West Point USA (1950 graduating class) men -- this is not an income/wealth/education/occupational-rank/social-dominance/SES status measure as defined for this review's status->reproduction extraction, so it would not qualify even if full text were available. The abstract states facial attractiveness negatively predicts age-specific reproduction in both sexes in Senegal and is unrelated to lifetime reproductive success in USA men, but no numeric effect sizes, N, or table data are present in the retrieved file.

This is a re-analysis/comment on Kanazawa (2003) using GSS, ISSP, and NHSLS data. Every regression table (Tables 1-8) has the dependent variable as either "number of sex partners" (lifetime, past 5 years, or past 12 months) or "frequency of sex in the last 12 months" (coital frequency) - proximate measures of mating effort/access, not actual reproduction. The paper never reports number of children, offspring, or completed fertility as an outcome. It references Perusse (1993)'s finding narratively (that status did not predict known fertility despite predicting potential conceptions) but does not itself estimate any status->fertility relationship. No status-to-reproduction effect is extractable.

reason_if_not: Pure narrative review (Stulp & Barrett 2016, Phil Trans R Soc B). It synthesizes prior literature on wealth-fertility but reports no original quantitative effect size: its own systematic component (a review of 13 longitudinal studies, refs [60-72]) gives only directional counts in the text ("eight positive, one negative and three null findings"), with no r/beta/OR/SE/N reported for any individual study -- full study-level detail is relegated to an electronic supplementary material file not present in the downloaded PDF. The single specific number in the text (Forbes-400 wealthy fathering "20-40% more children than the population average") is an imprecise range secondhand-cited to another paper (ref [94], Essock-Vitale 1984), not this paper's own analysis, and risks double-counting that primary source if it is separately catalogued. No defensible, independently attributable status->reproduction effect can be extracted from this source.

reason_if_not: This paper (Andersson, Jalovaara, Saarela & Uggla 2023, Proc. R. Soc. B, "A matter of time: Bateman's principles...") does not estimate a status->reproduction association. Its estimand is mating success (MS: cumulated number of unions, or cumulated union duration) predicting reproductive success (RS: number of children), per eq. 2.3 "RS = b0 + b1*MS + b2*Cohort" and the Poisson model in eq. 2.4. Income rank/quartile is used only as a STRATIFYING/INTERACTION variable to see whether the MS->RS (Bateman gradient) slope differs across income quartiles (Figures 2 and 3 report standardized beta of MS on RS, separately by income quartile and sex) -- it is never entered as the predictor of RS itself. The one place income enters descriptively (Figure 1a, "opportunity for selection" I = variance(RS)/mean(RS)^2 across income rank) is a variance ratio, not a correlation/beta/mean-level effect of income on number of children, so it is not usable as a poolable status->fertility effect size. No table in the 9-page main text (all data tables are in the electronic supplementary material S1-S8, not included in this PDF) reports a zero-order or adjusted coefficient of income, education, or any other status measure predicting number of children directly. Full text confirmed via pdftotext -layout scan of all 705 lines plus review of the results section (Figures 1-3 and surrounding text); no status->reproduction effect could be extracted.
